topics.name: Language Modeling Basics
topics.description: Language models are AI systems that learn to predict or generate text based on previous context; they form a fundamental building block in natural language processing, enabling applications like text generation and understanding.
prerequisites: None (basic understanding of machine learning concepts is helpful but not required)
topics.learning_objectives: Understand what a language model is and its purpose in NLP. Learn how language modeling involves predicting the next word in a sequence. Learn about simple approaches to language modeling (from basic n-gram models to neural network models) and how they generate text. See examples of text generated by language models. Appreciate why language modeling is a foundational task for more complex NLP applications.

topics.name: Transformer Architecture
topics.description: The Transformer is a neural network architecture based on self-attention that revolutionized language modeling by capturing long-range context and dependencies. It builds on the concept of language modeling introduced earlier (Topic 1) and serves as the backbone of modern large language models, enabling efficient training of very deep and large networks.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of neural networks and the concept of language modeling (Topic 1)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn why the Transformer architecture was developed and how it differs from previous sequence models (e.g., RNNs). Understand the key components of a Transformer (self-attention mechanism, multi-head attention, positional encoding, feed-forward layers) and how they work together. Learn how Transformers can process entire sequences in parallel and capture long-range relationships in text. Understand how the Transformer architecture enables scaling up to very large models and improved performance on NLP tasks.

topics.name: Pretraining and Fine-Tuning of Language Models
topics.description: Pretraining involves training a language model on massive general text data to learn broad language patterns, while fine-tuning is the process of adapting this pre-trained model to specific tasks or domains with additional targeted data. This topic connects the large-scale training of Transformers (Topic 2) with how models are later adapted for particular uses, establishing the pretrain-then-finetune paradigm.
prerequisites: Understanding of what language models are and how Transformers work (Topics 1 and 2)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what pretraining is and why it is done (to learn general language features from huge unlabeled text corpora). Understand the difference between pretraining and fine-tuning and how they complement each other. Learn about examples of pretraining tasks (such as next-word prediction or masked language modeling) and how these create a foundation of knowledge in the model. Understand how fine-tuning uses labeled or task-specific data to specialize the model for a particular task (for example, fine-tuning a general model for question-answering or translation). See examples of how fine-tuning can change a model’s behavior or improve performance on a task. Understand why fine-tuning is necessary to get the best performance on specific tasks and how it updates the model’s weights for that purpose.

topics.name: Need for Adaptation in LLMs (Static vs. Adaptive Models)
topics.description: Large language models are often static after their initial training, which means they struggle with new tasks or updated information that wasn’t in their training data. This topic explains why ongoing adaptation (continual learning) is important, building on the fine-tuning concept from Topic 3 and highlighting the limitations of keeping an LLM’s weights fixed when facing evolving needs.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of how models are trained and fine-tuned (Topic 3)
topics.learning_objectives: Understand what it means for a language model to be “static” (no weight updates after initial training). Learn about the problems that arise from a static model: outdated knowledge (the model doesn’t know about events or facts introduced after its training), inability to handle new or specialized tasks without additional training, and lack of personalization. Identify scenarios where model adaptation is needed – for example, incorporating new factual knowledge, adapting to a specific domain or jargon, or learning from user feedback over time. Understand the concept of continual learning (incrementally updating a model as new data comes in) and why it is challenging. Appreciate why automating the adaptation process would be beneficial (since manually re-training or fine-tuning models frequently is time-consuming and requires expertise).

topics.name: Adaptation Techniques for LLMs (Existing Approaches)
topics.description: Reviews the common methods used to update or adapt large language models with new data or tasks, such as standard fine-tuning on collected data, adding adapter modules, prompt-based few-shot learning, and using external knowledge sources. This topic is related to the previous discussion of adaptation needs (Topic 4) and sets the stage for a self-adapting approach by showing how adaptations are traditionally done with human intervention.
prerequisites: Good understanding of model training and why adaptation is needed (Topics 3 and 4)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn the standard fine-tuning approach for adapting an LLM to new data or a new task (full model gradient updates using a labeled dataset). Understand the concept of domain adaptation – fine-tuning a model on data from a new domain to improve its performance in that context. Learn about parameter-efficient tuning methods (such as adaptor layers or LoRA) that allow updating a small portion of the model’s parameters for quicker adaptation. Understand prompt-based adaptation: using few-shot prompts or prefix tuning to guide the model’s behavior without changing its weights. Learn about methods that incorporate external knowledge at runtime (for example, retrieval-augmented generation, where the model fetches relevant information instead of having to update its weights). Compare the pros and cons of these approaches (e.g., fine-tuning can be powerful but requires new training data and can cause forgetting, while prompting relies on context length and may be limited in effectiveness). Recognize that in all these traditional methods, the model itself does not decide how to change – the updates or prompts are provided by humans or separate systems.

topics.name: Reinforcement Learning (RL) Basics
topics.description: Reinforcement learning is a training paradigm where an agent learns to make decisions by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback in the form of rewards. This introduction to RL is included because the SEAL approach (to be discussed in Topic 7 onward) uses an RL loop to guide the model’s self-adaptation, so understanding how an agent can learn from reward signals will be important.
prerequisites: no prior knowledge of reinforcement learning is assumed
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what reinforcement learning is and how it differs from supervised learning (no direct “correct answer” for each step, instead learning from trial-and-error). Understand key concepts in RL: agent, environment, action, state, reward, and how these interact in a feedback loop. Learn about simple examples of RL (such as an agent learning to play a game or navigate a maze through rewards). Understand the concept of a policy (the agent’s strategy for choosing actions) and how it gets updated based on rewards (e.g., via policy gradients). See how reinforcement learning can be applied to train AI systems when you can measure performance with a reward, including an example in NLP (such as training a model with reinforcement learning from human feedback for better responses). Build intuition for why a reward-driven approach can help in scenarios where we want a model to learn behaviors that are not easily specified by direct supervision.

topics.name: Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) – Overview
topics.description: Introduces the concept of Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL), a framework in which a large language model can improve itself by generating its own fine-tuning data and instructions to update its parameters. This overview explains the high-level idea of how SEAL directly addresses the adaptation challenge discussed in Topic 4, using the model’s own outputs (instead of relying solely on external data or modules) to achieve continual learning.
prerequisites: Solid understanding of how LLMs are trained and adapted (Topics 3–5)
familiarity with reinforcement learning concepts (Topic 6) is also helpful
topics.learning_objectives: Understand the core idea of a self-adapting language model: a model that can adjust its own weights by training on data it generates itself. Learn the main components of the SEAL framework at a high level – for example, how the model produces a “self-edit” (a special output used for learning) and then uses it to update its own weights. Understand why this approach is novel compared to traditional adaptation methods (no external curated dataset or separate update module is needed – the model directs its own training). Learn the motivations behind SEAL, such as enabling an LLM to continuously learn new information or tasks after deployment. Be prepared to dive deeper into each part of the process (the self-edit generation, the fine-tuning update, and the reinforcement learning training loop) in subsequent topics.

topics.name: Self-Edit Generation Mechanism in SEAL
topics.description: Examines the first key component of the SEAL framework: how the model generates a “self-edit” given new input. In this step, the model takes the new information or task examples and produces a special output (the self-edit) that reformats or highlights the information, possibly suggests training examples or hyperparameters, and essentially serves as data for its own fine-tuning. This mechanism is closely related to the adaptation loop introduced in Topic 7, as it kick-starts the self-update process.
prerequisites: Understanding of the SEAL framework overview (Topic 7) and how fine-tuning works (Topic 3)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what a “self-edit” is in the context of SEAL and what form it can take. Understand how the model might restructure or rephrase new information, or generate question-answer pairs or other examples, as a way of creating training data for itself. See hypothetical examples of self-edits (for instance, given a new fact, the model might output a statement or QA pair that uses that fact, which can later be used to fine-tune the model). Understand that the self-edit can include instructions or parameters (for example, suggesting how to perform the update, such as how many gradient steps to take or what learning rate to use). Recognize why generating a useful self-edit is critical: it determines what knowledge or skill the model will learn in the next step. Appreciate how this step is the model essentially “deciding what to learn” from the new input.

topics.name: Self-Directed Fine-Tuning Process
topics.description: Describes how the model applies the self-edit output to perform an actual weight update, effectively fine-tuning itself with the data it generated. This topic builds on Topic 8 by explaining how the self-edit (containing new examples or instructions) is used in a supervised fine-tuning step to adjust the model’s parameters, making the adaptation persistent.
prerequisites: Understanding of the self-edit mechanism (Topic 8) and the standard fine-tuning process (Topic 3)
topics.learning_objectives: Understand the process of using the self-generated data (the self-edit) to update the model’s weights via gradient-based learning. Learn how supervised fine-tuning is carried out in this context, using the content the model produced as training examples or targets. Understand what it means for these weight updates to be persistent (the model retains the new knowledge or skill for future inputs). See how any instructions or hyperparameters suggested in the self-edit are applied during the update (for example, the model might specify to take a few gradient descent steps on a certain piece of text). Recognize the importance of balancing the update so that the model improves on the new information without forgetting its prior knowledge. Understand that this step completes one loop of self-adaptation: the model has now learned from the new input by incorporating it into its weights.

topics.name: Reinforcement Learning Loop in SEAL
topics.description: Discusses how a reinforcement learning approach is used to train the model to generate effective self-edits and updates. It builds on the RL basics from Topic 6 and ties together the self-edit and fine-tuning components (Topics 8 and 9) by treating the model’s adaptation process as an RL loop: the model’s action is producing a self-edit, and it receives a reward based on how well the updated model performs on the task or data of interest.
prerequisites: Good understanding of the self-adaptation process (Topics 7–9) and basic reinforcement learning concepts (Topic 6)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn why reinforcement learning is used in SEAL to train the model’s self-adaptation capability (as opposed to only supervised learning of the self-edit behavior). Understand how the self-edit generation can be viewed as the “action” of an agent (the model), and the improvement in performance after applying that edit is the “reward”. Learn the basics of how this RL loop is implemented: the model generates a self-edit, the self-edit is applied (updating the model’s weights), then the updated model is evaluated on a target task to produce a reward signal. Understand that the model’s parameters (specifically, the part that generates self-edits) are adjusted based on this reward to favor self-edits that lead to better performance (for example, using policy gradient methods to update the model’s behavior). Recognize the challenges involved, such as credit assignment (figuring out which aspect of the self-edit helped) and ensuring stability in training when the model is modifying itself. By the end, understand how the reinforcement learning loop gradually teaches the model to perform self-adaptation effectively, closing the loop of the SEAL framework.

topics.name: Knowledge Incorporation with Self-Adaptive LMs
topics.description: Explores an application of the SEAL approach for keeping a language model’s knowledge up-to-date by incorporating new information. This topic relates back to the motivation from Topic 4 (updating static models with new knowledge) and demonstrates how a self-adaptive model can ingest new facts or documents and update its parameters so that it can correctly use that information in the future.
prerequisites: Understanding of the SEAL method (Topics 7–10) and the importance of updating model knowledge (Topic 4)
topics.learning_objectives: Understand what it means to incorporate new knowledge into an LLM post-training (for example, learning a new fact or a recent event that was not in the original training data). Learn how the SEAL framework would handle this scenario: given new knowledge (such as a snippet of text with facts), the model generates a self-edit (which might summarize or extract Q&A pairs from that snippet) and then fine-tunes itself on that generated content. See a concrete example of knowledge incorporation (e.g., the model reads a new article about a recent event, creates training data from it, and after self-training is able to answer questions about that event accurately). Understand how the performance is measured here – for instance, checking if the model can recall or apply the new information correctly after the self-update. Compare this self-driven update to traditional approaches (like manually fine-tuning the model on the new article or using a retrieval system to fetch the article at query time). Appreciate the result: the model can maintain more up-to-date knowledge on its own, demonstrating one of the key benefits of self-adaptive learning.

topics.name: Few-Shot Generalization with Self-Adaptation
topics.description: Focuses on how self-adaptive language models tackle few-shot learning scenarios, where the model is given only a handful of examples of a new task. This topic builds on the idea of few-shot learning introduced earlier (Topic 5) and shows how the SEAL approach can convert a few provided examples into actual parameter updates, enabling the model to perform better on the new task than it would by just observing examples in context.
prerequisites: Familiarity with the concept of few-shot learning (Topic 5) and the SEAL adaptation process (Topics 7–10)
topics.learning_objectives: Understand what few-shot learning entails for language models (the model is provided  only a few example input-output pairs of a task and must generalize from them). Learn how the SEAL framework improves few-shot learning: instead of merely reading those examples as context, the model generates self-edits (additional training data or instructions derived from the examples) and fine-tunes itself on them. See an example scenario: given 5 examples of a new task (like translating a new language or a new format of question-answering), the model produces some generalized training data or rules and updates its weights, resulting in better performance on similar queries than if it only had the 5 examples in a prompt. Understand the difference in outcome: self-adaptation can lead to higher accuracy or more consistent results compared to standard in-context few-shot learning because the model has actually learned from the examples. Recognize the implications for sample efficiency – even with very little data, the model can meaningfully improve by training on it, illustrating a form of rapid learning. Review any results or findings from this use-case that were noted (such as how many examples are needed or how much improvement is seen with self-training vs. prompting).

topics.name: Comparison with Other Adaptation Methods
topics.description: Discusses how the self-adaptive approach (SEAL) compares to other methods of model adaptation and continual learning in the field. This topic ties back to the techniques covered in Topic 5, highlighting differences such as: SEAL uses the model’s own generated data vs. traditional fine-tuning uses externally provided data; SEAL integrates adaptation into the model’s generation process vs. other methods using separate modules or memory; and comparing the effectiveness and challenges of each approach.
prerequisites: Knowledge of the SEAL framework (Topics 7–10) and familiarity with traditional adaptation techniques (Topic 5)
topics.learning_objectives: Review other approaches to adapting models or enabling rapid learning: for example, standard fine-tuning, meta-learning algorithms (like MAML, which train models to adapt quickly with a few gradient steps), using adapter modules or LoRA for continual learning, online learning methods, and knowledge editing techniques. Compare each approach with SEAL in terms of mechanism: who provides the adaptation data (external vs. the model itself), how the model’s weights are updated (direct gradient updates vs. special parameter modules or none at all in prompting), and infrastructure needed (e.g., separate networks or memory systems). Understand the advantages of SEAL over some methods (it can autonomously decide how to update, potentially less human intervention needed) as well as its potential disadvantages (like requiring a more complex training setup with RL, or risk of the model going off-track if it learns incorrectly). See where SEAL fits in the broader landscape of making AI models more adaptive – for instance, how it complements ideas like retrieval (which avoids weight updates altogether) or how it differs from having a human in the loop (like in RLHF). By comparing these methods, solidify the understanding of what makes the self-adapting approach unique and how it addresses the adaptation problem.

topics.name: Future Directions and Challenges in Self-Adapting LMs
topics.description: Looks ahead at the open challenges and potential future developments for self-adapting language models. This concluding topic ties together what has been learned and encourages thinking about how the field might evolve – such as improving the stability and efficiency of self-learning, addressing safety concerns of models that update themselves, and exploring broader applications of the SEAL approach.
prerequisites: A comprehensive understanding of the current self-adaptation approach and context (all previous topics)
topics.learning_objectives: Reflect on the limitations of the current SEAL approach or self-adapting models (for example, computational cost of constant fine-tuning, or the possibility of the model drifting or learning incorrect information without oversight). Discuss potential improvements or enhancements to the method (such as incorporating validation checks, using human feedback to guide the self-training, or combining retrieval with self-adaptation for efficiency). Consider ethical and safety implications of models that can change their own behavior – ensuring they don’t evolve undesirable traits or that changes remain under control. Explore how the concept of self-adaptation could be applied beyond language models (perhaps to other domains like vision or robotics, where models might similarly learn on the fly). Summarize the key takeaways from the entire curriculum, ensuring a solid grasp of how self-adaptive language models work, why they are important, and what the learner can do next to further build on this knowledge.
